target: AG1's claim that AI is good for society because it improves convenience, health, productivity, accessibility, and safety.
objection: Those benefits are often outweighed by harms: AI can replace jobs and lower wages, weaken critical thinking and learning, reproduce racial bias, and create serious privacy risks. So AI is not inherently good for society.

target: AG2's claim that AI's harms mean it is not good for society.
objection: AG2's harms do not prove AI is not good overall; they only show it needs responsible governance. AI can augment workers, scaffold learning, be audited for bias, and be designed with privacy protections, so the risks do not overturn the societal benefits.

target: AG1's claim that AI can be made good for society through governance, retraining, audits, and privacy-preserving design.
objection: Those fixes are too unreliable in practice because the incentives favor speed and profit, oversight lags deployment, many systems are opaque, education safeguards are easy to bypass, and privacy controls still leave meaningful risk. Therefore AI is not reliably good for society.

target: AG2's claim that imperfect safeguards mean AI cannot be considered good for society.
objection: AI does not need perfect safeguards to be beneficial, because it is replacing imperfect human systems that already have bias, privacy, and safety failures. Audits, liability, procurement rules, and privacy-preserving techniques can shift incentives and improve outcomes relative to the status quo.

target: AG1's claim that audits, risk-tiered regulation, tutor-style use, and privacy controls can manage AI risks.
objection: Those controls often fail in practice: audits do not ensure accountability or understanding, automated systems can scale and accelerate bias, human review becomes rubber-stamping, and privacy protections are often undermined by power asymmetries and incentives. So AI remains not reliably good for society.

target: AG2's claim that governance cannot work reliably at scale.
objection: Governance can work through staged deployment, telemetry, rollback, documented rationales, appeal channels, and human review. Different AI use cases also have different risk profiles, so accessibility and safety tools should not be judged as if they are the same as high-stakes automated decision systems.

target: AG1's claim that monitoring, rollback, human review, and accessibility uses make AI net-good.
objection: Monitoring increases surveillance and privacy risk, rollback cannot undo all discrimination or unfair decisions, human review often becomes a bottleneck, and even lower-risk accessibility tools still depend on data processing and commercial platforms. So the mitigation methods do not make AI reliably good.

target: AG2's claim that monitoring and oversight inherently worsen privacy and cannot prevent harm.
objection: Monitoring can be privacy-preserving through aggregate metrics, short retention, access controls, and differential privacy; staged rollout and bias testing can prevent broader harm before deployment; human review can be structured rather than rubber-stamped; and accessibility benefits remain real even when some data is processed.

target: AG1's claim that privacy-preserving monitoring, pre-deployment testing, and human oversight can make AI safe enough.
objection: Privacy-preserving monitoring reduces accountability and may be too weak to detect discrimination, pre-deployment tests miss real-world and edge-case harms, proprietary opacity makes oversight performative, and incentives still push companies toward harmful deployment. So the proposed safeguards do not make AI reliably good.

target: AG2's claim that safeguards fail because incentives and opacity will always dominate.
objection: Society can change incentives through procurement rules, mandatory evaluations, and liability, and independent behavioral audits can create accountability even for proprietary systems. Because 'good for society' is about net impact relative to current baselines, AI can still be beneficial even with imperfect governance.

target: AG1's claim that procurement rules, liability, and audits can make AI safe enough.
objection: Those fixes will not scale across consumer apps, small businesses, and third-party integrations; audits are limited by vendor control and sampling; risk-tiering is easy to game; and AI can still amplify bias and displace workers faster than governance can react. Therefore AI is not reliably good for society.

target: AG2's claim that certification and liability cannot keep up with fast-changing AI deployment.
objection: AI's benefits are already real and concentrated in lower-risk domains, so governance does not need to be perfect to yield a net positive. Version-based re-certification, locked deployment pipelines, provenance, and stricter accessibility or education evaluation can make governance operational rather than merely aspirational.

target: AG1's claim that lower-risk AI uses like accessibility and education can be separated from the harmful ecosystem.
objection: In practice, lower-stakes and higher-stakes uses are entangled: they share data, models, and commercial infrastructure, so privacy and bias harms spill over. Benefits and harms are not cleanly separable, and the safest choice is to restrict AI broadly rather than promote it.

target: AG2's claim that spillover makes all AI effectively inseparable and harmful.
objection: Purpose limitation, compartmentalized pipelines, separate model instances, and enforceable audits can create real separation between low-risk and high-risk uses. Governance can also require disparate-impact testing so outcomes are judged by effects on different populations, not just averages.

target: AG1's claim that purpose limitation and compartmentalization can stop spillover.
objection: Those separation controls are difficult to enforce because data is processed through centralized multi-tenant systems, integration points spread it into analytics and recommendation tools, incentives favor repurposing, and impact testing only catches harm after it has already occurred. So separation is not reliable in practice.

target: AG2's claim that any imperfection in controls justifies broad restriction of AI.
objection: Risk-tiering and on-device or privacy-preserving designs can reduce spillover enough to preserve public-good uses like accessibility, health, and safety. AI should be treated as a portfolio of different risk levels rather than as a single uniformly harmful technology.

target: AG1's claim that low-risk AI can be safely contained through risk-tiering and privacy-preserving design.
objection: Even helpful AI creates centralized control, vendor lock-in, residual privacy risks, and incentive-driven risk classification. These systems entrench dependence and normalize a harmful ecosystem, so AI is not reliably good for society even in low-risk forms.

target: AG2's claim that centralized control and lock-in are inevitable.
objection: Interoperability, portability, local or user-controlled modes, and accessibility-first standards can reduce lock-in and centralized control. AI can still be good for society if users are not trapped in one vendor's ecosystem and if performance and transparency requirements are enforced.

target: AG1's claim that portability and user controls solve lock-in and privacy concerns.
objection: Porting data does not port the proprietary model behavior that creates the real benefit, privacy settings are often cosmetic or bundled, and accessibility standards do not stop broader harms like labor displacement or bias. So these fixes do not make AI reliably good for society.

target: AG2's claim that privacy settings and interoperability are insufficient.
objection: Independent certification, continuous compliance, integration-level restrictions, separate model instances, and outcome-based reporting can prevent spillover better than simple user opt-outs. If these controls are mandatory, AI can still deliver accessibility and safety benefits while limiting harm.

target: AG1's claim that certification and compliance can keep pace with AI deployment.
objection: Certification cannot keep up with frequent model updates, audits certify paperwork rather than real outcomes, vendors can strategically comply around tests, and even certified accessibility systems can still bias or surveil users and contribute to learning erosion. So AI is not reliably good for society.

target: AG2's claim that stronger operational safeguards still will not make AI good.
objection: Operational safeguards can be made version-based and technically enforced, with signed model builds, change logs, provenance, contractual telemetry, meaningful liability, and fairness evaluation for accessibility and education. These measures can keep AI beneficial while controlling harm.

target: AG1's claim that version-locked deployment, provenance, liability, and evaluation are enough.
objection: Those safeguards increase surveillance, do not scale across the broader AI ecosystem, and still cannot prevent compounding harms before they occur. Liability only compensates after harm, and education tools still tend to drift toward answer-substitution, undermining critical thinking. So AI remains not reliably good.

target: AG2's claim that broad restriction is the safest response because governance cannot keep up.
objection: Broad restriction would impose large opportunity costs by reducing accessibility, health, and workplace safety benefits that are real now. The better response is selective, risk-tiered governance that preserves low-risk benefits while focusing restrictions on the highest-stakes uses.
